question: Which of the following can be blocked by atropine, a muscarinic receptor blocker?

options.opa: Increased blood pressure caused by nicotine
options.opb: Increased skeletal muscle strength caused by neostigmine, an acetycholine esterase inhibitor
options.opc: Bradycardia caused by infusion of acetylcholine

reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "Atropine" -> "blocks muscarinic receptors" -> "prevents acetylcholine action on heart" -> "prevents bradycardia" -> 95%
CHAIN: "Atropine" -> "blocks muscarinic receptors" -> "no effect on nicotinic receptors" -> "no effect on nicotine-induced blood pressure increase" -> 70%
CHAIN: "Atropine" -> "blocks muscarinic receptors" -> "no effect on skeletal muscle" -> "no effect on neostigmine-induced muscle strength increase" -> 70%
CHAIN: "Atropine" -> "blocks muscarinic receptors" -> "prevents acetylcholine action on heart" -> "prevents bradycardia" -> "no effect on nicotine or neostigmine actions" -> 85%
analysis: Atropine is a muscarinic receptor antagonist, meaning it blocks the action of acetylcholine at muscarinic receptors. Muscarinic receptors are primarily found in the heart, smooth muscles, and glands. Atropine is known to counteract bradycardia (slow heart rate) caused by acetylcholine because this effect is mediated through muscarinic receptors in the heart. Nicotine primarily acts on nicotinic receptors, which are not affected by atropine, so atropine cannot block the increased blood pressure caused by nicotine. Similarly, neostigmine increases skeletal muscle strength by inhibiting acetylcholinesterase, leading to increased acetylcholine at nicotinic receptors in the neuromuscular junction, which atropine does not block. Therefore, the most likely correct option is that atropine can block bradycardia caused by acetylcholine infusion, but not the other effects.
